subject: computer-science
title: RISC vs CISC and Cache Hierarchies
welcome_lead: Two design philosophies — and the layers of memory that feed them.
meta_desc: A-Level CS: RISC, CISC, cache levels L1/L2/L3 and locality.
final_note: Cache and instruction design together decide real performance.

concepts.def: Reduced Instruction Set Computer — simple, fast instructions.
Complex Instruction Set Computer — fewer, more powerful instructions.
The fastest, smallest cache, on-chip with the CPU core.
Larger, slightly slower cache, often per-core.
Largest, slowest cache, shared between cores.
Tendency to reuse nearby memory addresses soon after access.

walkthroughs.body_html: RISC (ARM) uses many simple instructions of fixed length — easy to pipeline. CISC (x86) uses fewer, more powerful instructions of varied length. Modern x86 chips translate CISC into RISC-like micro-ops internally.
L1 is smallest and fastest (tens of KB). L2 is bigger (hundreds of KB). L3 is shared across cores (megabytes). Each level trades capacity for latency.
Programs exhibit temporal locality (reusing the same address) and spatial locality (using nearby addresses). Caches exploit both by keeping recent and adjacent data close to the CPU.
